sections.html:
Morgan County sits in north central Georgia with Madison as its seat. Demand for homes here is driven by easy reach of Lake Oconee and four job centers: Atlanta, Athens, Augusta and Macon. The county had 22,095 residents in July 2025, up 10.0% from the April 2020 base, and 9,489 housing units. About 78.2% of homes are owner-occupied, and the typical owner-occupied home is valued at $342,300.

Madison, Bostwick and Rutledge are cities and Buckhead is a town. Madison levies its own city tax on top of the county's, so an owner inside the city limits has two bills to settle when selling.

sections.h2: Which two offices handle Morgan County property tax?
sections.html:
Two desks share the work. One sends and collects the bill; the other decides what your house is worth and who gets an exemption.

The Tax Commissioner collects property, mobile home and timber taxes, sells and renews car tags (online renewal is available), and processes title transfers. Bring a Georgia driver's license or ID showing a Morgan County address when you go in person.

The Tax Assessor's office is at 150 E Washington Street, Suite 130, Madison, GA 30650. It takes returns and homestead applications, and the filing window for returns runs January 2 to April 1. Value challenges start at that desk and can go on to the Board of Equalization, whose members are appointed by the grand jury.

The county Board of Commissioners sets the county budget and mill rate. The Board of Education recommends a school rate that the commissioners must levy with very few exceptions. The state's own levy is capped at one fourth of a mill.

sections.h2: Due date and how to pay
sections.html:
Morgan County's official property tax deadline is November 15, after which penalties and interest begin. Georgia's default is December 20, but a county may move it to December 1 or November 15, and Morgan chose the earliest.

You can pay online through the county's online tax payment system. The state adds a 60 day grace period counted from the bill's postmark, so read the bill itself before assuming a date. The same office collects mobile home and timber tax, so ask the counter for those due dates.

A buyer who closes after January 1 should confirm who carries that year's bill, because under state rules the January 1 owner is the one liable.

Morgan County layers several exemptions on top of the state basics, and a long-time owner may qualify for more than one. The Tax Assessor decides eligibility.

  • Standard homestead: as much as $2,000 comes off the assessed value, which is 40% of market value, for county, school and state operating levies.
  • Age 65 and up: a further $10,000 comes off the county and school operating portion, with no income test.
  • Madison residents over 65: another $10,000 off for city maintenance and operations tax.
  • Standard elderly: up to $4,000 off for owners 65 and older whose net income with a spouse stays at or below $10,000, with Social Security and some retirement income excluded.
  • Age 65 and older, state portion: the home and up to 10 acres are exempt from the state's levy in full.
  • Disabled veteran rated 100% service connected: a larger deduction that changes every year, with a DD214 and a VA rating letter required.
  • Surviving spouses: up to $50,000 for an unremarried spouse of a service member who died in war or armed conflict, and a full exemption for the unremarried spouse of a firefighter or peace officer who died in the line of duty.

sections.h2: How do I file or keep a homestead exemption?
sections.html:
Take the application to the Tax Assessor. You can drop it off at any time, but April 1 ends the window for the current year, and the house must have been your residence on New Year's Day.

Approval is not a yearly chore. Once granted, the exemption rolls forward by itself. You file again only after a change of ownership, a move, a switch to a different kind of exemption, or when the exemption depends on income. If the Board of Assessors denies an application, the county must notify you, and you can appeal. Farmland owners can ask the assessor about conservation use, and business owners about personal property.

After the Board of Tax Assessors mails a notice that a value has changed, you have 45 days to respond. The board looks again and sends back its decision. If you still disagree, the next stage is a Board of Equalization hearing, unless you chose arbitration when you first filed.

Gather what you have before you file: a recent appraisal, sale prices of similar homes nearby, and photos of any defects that lower the value. Written evidence carries more weight than a general complaint that the number feels high.

Three grounds are allowed: taxability, value, and how the value compares with similar properties. Complaints about the size of the bill do not count, and a late filing is barred. Superior court stays open after the administrative step. A new return filed during the January 2 to April 1 window can set a different value and protect your appeal rights if the board raises it again.

sections.h2: Other county departments that touch a sale
sections.html:
Planning and Development handles zoning, flood plain management, a fee schedule and the comprehensive plan. Look at the zoning and flood plain pages before listing a lot that sits near water, because buyers and lenders will ask. Roads and Bridges publishes a mowing schedule and a road resurfacing list.

Court Services covers Magistrate Court, Probate Court and Superior Court, which matters if you are selling an inherited house. Solid Waste and Sanitation includes recycling.

Start by requesting a payoff figure from the Tax Commissioner's office, and have the closing attorney say who covers the November 15 bill when a sale closes earlier. The Department of Revenue says no refund exists for part of a year, so proration lives in the contract.

A Madison address adds a city bill, so ask which office collects it. Sellers over 65 should check that their exemptions are on the account before the buyer's lender reviews the tax figures. Buyers who will occupy the home file their own application, again by April 1.

A simple order of work: first ask the Tax Commissioner for the balance on the account, then ask the Tax Assessor to confirm which exemptions are active, then hand both to the closing attorney. Doing this early avoids surprises on closing day, since the attorney needs the payoff before preparing the settlement statement.

A cash sale skips the lender's tax review and the wait for an appraisal, which can help when a bill is already past due. The title company still collects whatever is owed from the proceeds at closing.

faqs.q: What is Morgan County's property tax deadline?
faqs.a: November 15, after which penalties and interest build.

faqs.q: Who takes Morgan County homestead applications?
faqs.a: The Tax Assessor, at 150 E Washington Street, Suite 130, in Madison. Aim for April 1 if you want the savings this year.

faqs.q: Can I pay Morgan County property tax online?
faqs.a: Yes, through the county's online tax payment system, which the Tax Commissioner's page links to.

faqs.q: Does Morgan County give seniors an extra exemption?
faqs.a: Yes. Residents 65 and older can take an additional $10,000 off assessed value for county and school maintenance and operations, with no income limit. Madison residents can add the same amount for city tax.

faqs.q: How many days do I have to appeal in Morgan County?
faqs.a: Forty-five, counted from the notice of changed value. The Board of Tax Assessors hears it first.
